articleTitle: The operation and maintenance of class ie electric locomotives: Natal 3000-volt D.C main line electrification
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The above paper quite cleariy results from a long and careful study of practical pro blems encountered in the operation of these locomotives and congratulations are due to Mr Lehman for having succeeded in embodying so much within the compass of his paper which makes it a useful source . of reference. The following comments are offered with regard to the regenerative braking. On page 249 there is obviously a printer's error in line (2). The first paragraph further states that by cutting out portions of the stabilizing resistor, a higher regenerated current is obtained. This is not necessarily the case. By cutting out parts of the stabilizing resistor, the field current rises and the speed thus decreases thereby reducing the regenerated current for the same doad and gradient. It is believed that drivers frequently use this P 16 notch in order to reduce the speed of the train when passing through a crossing in regeneration. A higher regenerated current is obtained only if there is an increase in the load or the gradient which may yield a speed beyond the range of the full stabilizing resistor notches.

Theso two loops of six turns each are connected in opposition, with a Grassot fluxInoter in shunt. A deflection of the fluxmeter is convcrt.t:\d to an audible warning by means of a photo tube, amplifier relay and alarm bell. A midget submarine 50 feet long entering at 3 knots will produce an indication of some 10 seconds duration when ovor either loop; and these indications will be separated by an interval of 110 seconds duration while the submarine is between the two loops. articleTitle: Lighthouses and other aids to navigation
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: In his first query Mr Milton raises a point of great importance. AB a general rule, any light source designed for operation with a system of lenses is made as small as possible, the H point source being assumed in roost calculations. In a system of revolving lenses, designed for service in a lighthouse, the divergence of the beam is of the greatest importance, for the length of the :flash is directly proportioned to this divergence. Ideally, the length of flash should he long enough for the eye to turn to the light and to place it in focus. It takes about 02 seconds for the eye to do this, and hence the minimum length of flash should be of this order. Where there is a quick succession of flashes. the length of each :flash may be considerably reduced, and quick-flashing lights in which the length of :flash is only 01 second are in general use. In a large revolving light, flashes of even 01 second duration a.re difficult to obtain, for if the power rating of the lamp be held constant and the projected area of the filament be increased, the avera.ge brightness of the filament is decreased, and as a result of the wider spacing of the filaments, the light source is not evenly illuminated. In extreme cases of this nature, the resulting variations in intensity of the beam, may result in a double beam being seen at the extreme range of the light.

articleTitle: Waveform in electrical engineering
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: It must be obvious to all students of alternating theory that the work is based on the fact that the variation of the various quantities with time can be expressed by a sine function. The reason for this use of sine functions a.nd the assumptions bound up therein are never sufficiently well treated . in the majority of text books on the subject. It is the object of this short paper to discuss this point in some detail, and to show how the theory developed is limited by the assumptions made. It is also proposed to discuss how the theory may be extended by the use of Fouriers Series.

articleTitle: The magnetic mine problem in South Africa
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The paper is introduced by a brief survey of terrestial magnetism, and the effect it produces in iron ships. The four main methods of compensating for these phenomena are then dealt with, and it is shown how Allied ships were gradually more and more efficiently demagnetized as the late war progressed. Instances of how the time of operation to degauss ships in local waters was progressively reduced are mentioned.

articleTitle: Communications network of the union of south africa
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The magnitude of the problem of handling constantly increasing traffic necessitates straight thinking years before the projects mature. The progress that is being made to-day is due to the correctness of decisions made by the Department of Posts and Telegraphs and engineers abroad as far back as 1936. This advance planning must go on as a continuous process—at least until there are some indications of satura tion—a state of, affairs which no tele communications man has ever yet exper ienced. Hence, this paper does, I think, afford a timely opportunity to consider briefly the possible trend of future activities. So far as open-wire routes are concerned, it would appear that the conventional type of construction prevents exploitation at frequencies above 150 kilocycles per second, certainly with the equipment that is at present available. Such a route and systems can provide approximately 130 telephone channels between primary centres. Present plans envisage, say, forty tele phone channels between Johannesburg and Bloemfontein and Johannesburg to Pietermaritzburg. It is my own opinion that within a few years certain primary centres may require more than 130 telephone channels linking them. How could this need be met by using systems which are at present developed.

articleTitle: A practical analysis of induction motor faults and failures
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: It is, I think, generally accepted that all machinery which has td operate' underground in a gold mine has to withstand the most severe conditions, as well as in some cases very rough handling—sometimes unavoidably—in getting the particular piece of apparatus to the site of operation. These conditions apply in full to induction motors. Many cast iron motor frames are broken or cracked, especially at the feet, while being tra.nsported for installation underground in the most awkward pla.ces. It would therefore a.ppear that the fabricated steel frame has a definite advantage over the cast iron frame for this particular application.

articleTitle: Some notes on mines and mine sweeping
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The notes first deal in general terms with the principles of operation of contact, antenna, controlled and magnetic types of moored mines. German ground mines used in the recent war are then described, followed by brief particulars of some of the many types of sweeps developed to deal with the magnetically operated ground mine. The “L” magnetic sweep is then described in more detail, and the notes conclude with descriptions of the two types of sweep adopted to deal with the acoustic type of ground mine.

articleTitle: The relative merits of frequency modulation and amplitude modulation as applied to a broadcasting service
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: This paper discusses the use of frequency modulation as a subsidiary transmission to the present medium wave broadcasting service. It is shown that frequency modulation has definite advantages over corresponding amplitude modulated systems, and particular emphasis is laid on the increased signal-to-noise ratio resulting from the use of frequency modulation. The paper discusses the inter-station interference for the two types of transmissions and the essential differences between frequency and amplitude modulated receivers and transmitters are given, with particular reference to equipment built by the South African Broadcasting Corporation.

Mention is made of other types of mercury are rectifier, such as the glass bulb, the pumped, water-cooled type and the ignitron, each of which has a sphere of application.
